title: Multiobjective variational quantum optimization for constrained problems: an application to Cash Management
abstract_summary: The paper introduces MOVCO, a Multi-Objective Variational Constrained Optimizer that combines variational quantum algorithms with a multiobjective genetic optimizer (NSGA-II) to handle hard constraints in combinatorial problems. The method is applied to a newly formulated Cash Management Problem, and empirical results show MOVCO outperforms standard penalty-based VQE by better satisfying constraints, avoiding infeasible local minima, and reducing transaction costs.
methodology_description: The authors propose MOVCO (Multi-Objective Variational Constrained Optimizer), a hybrid quantum-classical approach for constrained combinatorial optimization. MOVCO wraps a variational quantum algorithm (here VQE with a hardware-efficient ansatz or a separable product ansatz) with a classical multi-objective genetic optimizer (NSGA-II). The genetic optimizer treats each candidate variational parameter vector as an individual and simultaneously optimizes two fitness functions: (1) the percentage of constraints satisfied by the sampled bitstrings from the variational state (P(θ)); and (2) a restricted energy estimator computed only over sampled states that satisfy all constraints (normalized E(θ)). The quantum component evaluates the ansatz by drawing K measurement shots to produce sampled classical states; costs and constraint satisfaction are computed classically from those samples. NSGA-II ranks individuals by Pareto dominance (non-dominated front sorting and crowding distance) and generates offspring via binary tournament selection, simulated binary crossover (SBX) and polynomial mutation. MOVCO is benchmarked against a standard VQE baseline that encodes constraints as penalty terms in the Hamiltonian and uses SPSA or a single-objective genetic optimizer for parameter updates. Experiments are classical, noise-free simulations using randomly generated instances of a Cash Management Problem (CMP), and performance is measured by metrics such as proportion of constraints satisfied, approximation ratio, and success rate (overlap with global optimum).
experimental_setup: Classical, noise-free statevector / circuit simulation. Each evaluation draws K = 8192 measurement samples to emulate finite-shot measurements. Experiments executed on HPC resources (DRAGO supercomputer via SGAI-CSIC and Finis Terrae at CESGA).
dataset_used: Synthetic Cash Management Problem (CMP) instances generated by the authors. Instances encode C cash points over D days with discretized cash levels; parameters (sending/withdrawing costs, initial cash predictions) are drawn from simple discrete uniform distributions as specified in the paper.

experiment_input.generation_procedure: For each cash point c and day d: sending/withdrawal price kc drawn uniformly in [1,4] (first-day price doubled). Initial predictions pct drawn uniformly in integer interval [-2,5]. Other parameters: discrete cash levels (h=4 used typically), Am normalization, max total cash vf set to C in some experiments, daily transaction limit l set depending on C. Instances generated randomly following described rules.
experiment_input.instance_counts_and_sizes: Small-scale benchmarks: 120 random instances for C=2 over D in {2,3,4} days (qubit counts V = 2*C*D reported). Larger-scale experiments: single random instances for C in [10..22] and D=7 (week), up to V ≈ 308 qubits/variables.
experiment_input.preprocessing: Encoding of CMP to an Ising/Pauli-Z Hamiltonian with binary-spin encoding per discretized cash level. Constraints expressed as classical checks on sampled states and also as operators for theoretic definition; for penalty baseline, Heaviside penalties added to Hamiltonian with tuned penalty constants.

pipeline_steps: 1) Generate synthetic CMP instance(s) with chosen C and D and discretization parameters.
2) Map CMP to a Pauli-Z Hamiltonian (binary encoding of discretized cash levels).
3) Initialize a population of candidate variational parameter vectors (angles). For hardware-efficient ansatz, parameters initialized near pi/4; for product ansatz, independent single-qubit angles.
4) For each candidate (per generation) run the variational circuit (classical simulation) and draw K=8192 measurement samples; compute per-sample classical costs and constraint checks.

5) Compute two fitness values per candidate: P(θ) = fraction of sampled bitstrings satisfying constraints; E(θ) = restricted normalized energy computed only over sampled states within the feasible subspace (using an efficiently computed upper bound of cost for normalization).

6) Apply NSGA-II: non-dominated sorting into Pareto fronts; compute crowding distances; select parents by binary tournament; produce offspring via SBX crossover and polynomial mutation; offspring size equals population size.
7) Iterate generations (typical experiments used population=10, up to several hundred generations; larger problems used population=100 and up to 10,000 quantum-evaluation-equivalents in comparisons).

8) Baseline runs: run a penalized VQE where constraints are added as penalty terms to the Hamiltonian and optimize parameters with SPSA (gradient-free, two circuit evaluations per iteration) or with a single-objective GA using same genetic operators for fair comparison.

9) Collect metrics: constraint satisfaction percentage P(θ), approximation ratio, success rate (overlap with global minimum > 0.1 for small problems where global min known), distributions over instances, and Pareto-front evolution.
experiment_process.parameters_and_iterations: Small experiments: population size = 10, offspring = 10, number of generations varied (plots up to ~400 generations); shots per evaluation K = 8192; ansatz: single-layer hardware-efficient with Ry rotations and nearest-neighbor CZ entanglers; L = 1 commonly used. Baseline SPSA runs with up to ~500 iterations for penalty tuning, and up to thousands of evaluations in comparisons. Penalty hyperparameters tuned empirically (Af = A = 25 chosen). Larger experiments: separable product-state ansatz (no entanglement), population=100 for MOVCO, penalty A values up to 50 for baseline, comparisons performed by number of quantum-evaluation-equivalents (e.g., MOVCO's population evaluations vs SPSA's two per iteration).

experiment_output.result_formats: Per-instance numerical metrics and distributions (time series of Pareto-front points across generations, boxplots, percent-success counts, plots of constraint satisfaction vs restricted energy).
metrics_reported: P(θ): percentage of sampled states satisfying all constraints
Approximation ratio e(θ) = (Cmax - ⟨C⟩) / (Cmax - Cmin) with normalization defined in paper
Success rate: probability/overlap of sampling global minimum (⟨|⟨v(θ)|gs⟩|^2⟩ > 0.1 for small instances)
Distributional statistics across instances (mean, 2.5–97.5 percentiles, boxplots)

VQE with penalty-augmented Hamiltonian optimized by single-objective genetic algorithm
experiment_output.observed_outputs: MOVCO shows higher rate of reaching feasible solutions (P≈1), improved approximation ratios on average, reduced dispersion, and higher probability of sampling global minima for tested CMP instances compared to penalized VQE baselines.

key_findings: [supported] MOVCO (Multi-Objective Variational Constrained Optimizer) is introduced: a hybrid variational method that uses a genetic multi-objective optimizer (NSGA-II) to simultaneously maximize constraint satisfaction (percentage P) and minimize a restricted in-constraint energy estimator (E).

[supported] In noise-free classical simulations on a realistic cash-management formulation (Cash Management Problem, CMP), MOVCO more reliably converges to feasible (constraint-satisfying) low-cost solutions than a standard VQE approach that encodes constraints via penalty terms.

[supported] For small CMP instances (120 random instances with 2 cash points over 2–4 days, mapped to up to 16 qubits) MOVCO reached full constraint satisfaction (P ~ 1) for all instances after ~200 generations and achieved high approximation ratios (most instances > 0.8).

[supported] In direct comparisons on 120 CMP instances (2 cash points, 4 days, 16-qubit problems) MOVCO produced (i) a higher fraction of instances where almost all sampled solutions were feasible (P>0.99), (ii) higher probability of sampling the global minimum (overlap>0.1), (iii) higher average approximation ratio and lower dispersion, compared to VQE with penalty terms optimized by SPSA or a single-objective GA.

[supported] For larger CMP instances using a product (separable) ansatz (tested up to V=308 binary variables), MOVCO outperformed penalized VQE in constraint-satisfaction gap and transaction-cost gap; authors report MOVCO produced better solutions for 100% of tested instances after 10,000 evaluations in that setup.

[supported] All numerical experiments reported were classical, noise-free simulations; typical sampling used K=8192 measurement shots per evaluated circuit; small hardware-efficient entangling ansatz (one layer) was used for entangled tests, and a separable product ansatz for larger instances.
[speculative] MOVCO is ansatz-agnostic and could be applied to other variational algorithms (e.g., QAOA, layer-VQE) and hardware implementations.

[speculative] The method could be extended (e.g., CVaR-style energy, limiting percentage of feasible samples, hyperparameter tuning) to further improve performance on constrained combinatorial problems.
[speculative] The authors claim this is among the first variational-method studies targeting realistic constrained optimization problems of this type (CMP).
results_summary: The paper proposes MOVCO, a hybrid variational optimization scheme that uses NSGA-II to jointly maximize constraint satisfaction and minimize a restricted energy estimated only over sampled feasible states. In noise-free classical simulations on a novel spin formulation of the Cash Management Problem, MOVCO consistently converged to feasible, low-cost solutions more reliably than a standard VQE that uses penalty terms to enforce constraints. For small instances (up to 16 qubits) MOVCO reached full feasibility across tested instances within a few hundred generations and achieved high approximation ratios; in larger tests using a separable ansatz (up to 308 binary variables) MOVCO also outperformed penalized VQE in both feasibility and cost metrics. All results are from classical simulations (no hardware/noise).
performance_claims: [supported] In 120 random CMP instances with 2 cash points and optimization windows of 2–4 days (up to 16 qubits), MOVCO achieved full constraint satisfaction (P ~ 1) for all instances after ~200 generations.

[supported] For the same 120-instance suite, approximately 80% of instances (2 cash points, 4 days) and ~90% (2 cash points, 3 days) allowed the MOVCO-trained wavefunction to sample the global minimum with overlap > 0.1 after ~100 generations.
[supported] Most tested small instances achieved approximation ratios > 0.8 under MOVCO; plots show success rates for thresholds 0.95, 0.9, 0.85, 0.8 increasing with generations.

[supported] In 120-instance comparisons (2 cash points, 4 days), MOVCO produced a higher fraction of instances with nearly all sampled solutions feasible (P>0.99) and higher average approximation ratios than VQE with penalty terms (penalty hyperparameters tuned; optimizer SPSA or single-objective GA).

[supported] In larger experiments using product (separable) ansatz up to V=308 variables, the authors report MOVCO produced better solutions for 100% of tested instances after 10,000 quantum-circuit evaluations (compared to penalized VQE).

[supported] Simulation details: experiments were noise-free classical simulations, sampling K=8192 bitstrings per circuit evaluation; MOVCO used NSGA-II with population sizes (10 for small tests, 100 for large tests) and standard GA operators.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper reports empirical improvements of a classical+variational hybrid heuristic (MOVCO) over penalty-based variational optimization in noise-free classical simulations of combinatorial instances. It does not claim or demonstrate a quantum computational advantage (no provable speedup and no noisy-hardware results); improvements are algorithmic/heuristic within VQA-style methods and shown by simulation.
limitations: Constraints of realistic practical problems can be too difficult to map natively to quantum hardware, motivating indirect approaches (author-stated).
Standard penalty methods require instance-dependent hyperparameter tuning and do not guarantee convergence to feasible solutions due to existence of infeasible local minima (author-stated).

MOVCO can be ineffective when the subspace of states satisfying none of the constraints is very large; this can produce effective barren-plateau-like behavior where the restricted energy is trapped at 0 because sampling feasible states is too unlikely (author-stated).
Numerical experiments were performed using noise-free classical simulation; the effect of real device noise and finite-sampling noise on MOVCO's performance was not evaluated (inferred).

Demonstrations with entangling ansatzes are limited in size by exponential cost of classical simulation; larger-instance experiments required switching to fully separable (product) ansatzes, so scalability of entangling ansatz + MOVCO on larger problems remains untested (author-stated and inferred).

[inferred] MOVCO requires many circuit evaluations per generation (population-size evaluations), which increases quantum resource demands compared with low-query optimizers; although parallel evaluation is possible, total resource cost may be high in practice.
[inferred] There are no formal theoretical guarantees provided for convergence to global feasible optima (or rates); performance claims are empirical.
[inferred] The approach assumes the ability to efficiently check constraint satisfaction for each sampled classical state; for some problems this check itself could be costly or nontrivial.

The influence of MOVCO's genetic-algorithm hyperparameters (population size, selection/crossover/mutation choices) was not fully explored; tuning might be required for best performance (author-stated).

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — MOVCO integrates a variational quantum circuit (VQE-style ansatz) with a classical multi-objective genetic optimizer (NSGA-II) that optimizes constraint satisfaction P(θ) and a restricted normalized energy E(θ) in parallel.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The genetic optimizer treats variational parameter vectors as individuals and uses sampled bitstrings (K=8192 shots) from the quantum state to compute fitness, guiding Pareto-based selection and operator-driven offspring generation (SBX, polynomial mutation).

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Method targets NISQ-friendly components (hardware-efficient and separable product ansatzes, low-depth circuits L=1, finite-shot evaluation) and frames a practical constrained-optimization workflow for near-term devices, although not demonstrated on hardware.

#idea:hybrid-approach — In classical, noise-free simulations on synthetic Cash Management Problem (CMP) instances, MOVCO outperforms a standard penalty-based VQE baseline (with SPSA or single-objective GA) in constraint satisfaction, avoiding infeasible local minima and improving objective metrics (approximation ratio, success rate).
#limitation:simulation-only — All reported experiments are classical, noise-free statevector/circuit simulations (HPC), no runs on real QPUs were performed.

#limitation:no-empirical-validation — Larger-scale experiments are limited (single random instances for up to ~308 variables) and baselines rely on empirically tuned penalties; no real-world financial data or hardware validation provided.

#limitation:qubit-count — Although experiments report up to ~308 binary variables in simulation, these use separable product ansatzes and single-instance tests, so reported scale may not reflect practical hardware feasibility.

#limitation:data-encoding — The approach depends on a discretized binary encoding of cash levels (one-hot/binary spin per level), but the costs and scalability implications of this encoding (resolution vs. qubit overhead) are not fully explored empirically.
